name: Dschang
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Bird, Steven. 1999. Dschang syllable structure. In Harry van der Hulst & Nancy A. Ritter (eds.), The Syllable: Views and Facts, 447-476. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter. [author preprint 'Dschang Syllable Structure', dated May 1997, cogprints 2183; open the Internet Archive copy ofhttp://cogprints.org/2183/3/syllable.pdf]
catalog_locator: Preprint p. 1 (sec. 1 Introduction, and fn. 2), p. 25 (sec. 6 Loanword Phonology, exx. 38a-b) and p. 26 (ex. 41e); pagination confirmed by the running heads 'Steven Bird 25' and '26 Dschang Syllable Structure'; p. 25 also checked as a. Published version pp. 447-476 not opened.
catalog_quote: The considerable interest in the language has focussed almost solely on tone, stemming from work by Hyman & Tadadjeu (1976). However, the language is also interesting for its syllable structure. [...] In this and subsequent displays, acute and grave accent symbolise high and low tone respectively. The exclamation point symbolises downstep. Final low tones are falling unless marked with a degree symbol. [...] The English stress is usually preserved in the tone melody of the word (38a), though not always (38b). [...] Generalising across these two cases, we can observe that high tone is assigned to the penultimate vowel. [...] Finally, in (41e) we see the loss of a vowel when a reduced form satisfies the syllable structure of the language, possibly in order to mimic the stress pattern of kerosene.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Yemba/Dschang is described as a tone language (high vs. low tone plus downstep; three-level H/M/L marking in the orthography). No opened source states a word-stress rule or discusses stress in native words. The only stress-related remarks are (a) Bird 1999: English stress in loanwords is normally mapped onto the tone melody, surfacing as high tone on the penultimate vowel of the loan; and (b) Faytak & Steffman 2023 (p. 198), reporting Hyman 1985: 48, that the first syllable of the stem is the phonologically prominent position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Bird 1999 (38b): some loans (akaleta 'carrot', akalatusi 'eucalyptus', afrepan 'frypan') do not preserve the English stress in their tone melody.
new_statements.domain_note: Loanword adaptation only (Bird); stem-initial phonological prominence (Faytak & Steffman after Hyman 1985) concerns the stem, not the phonological word; Bird's data are from the main northern (Bafou) dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources treat Yemba = Dschang = Bamileke-Dschang (ISO ybb, yemb1246). Bird 1999 states (fn. 1) that his data come from 'the main northern dialect, spoken in Bafou and elsewhere'; Assoumou 1991 covers the Foreke-Dschang variety; Nanfah 2006 delimits the Yemba dialects (Bafou, Foreke-Dschang, Bamendou, Fongo-Tongo, etc.) without separate glottocodes.

[pages not established; also posted on Academia.edu item 27942444]
tone_statements.quote: Like so many languages in the world, Yemba is a tone language. ... a. lètɔ́ŋ “nib” b. lètɔ̄ŋ “read” c. lètɔ̀ŋ “navel” These words have the same consonants and vowels, placed in the same order. The vowel ɔ in the second syllable carries the high, mid and low tones in the three words respectively. ... Tadadjeu and Tegomo-Nguetse (1972), distinguish 5 fundamental tones in Yémba, namely: - Three simple: high ( ´ ), mid ( ̄ ) and low ( ̀ ) ; - Two modulated: high-low tone ( ^ ) and low-high tone ( ̌ ).
tone_statements.summary: Author works with three level tones H, M, L on each vowel/syllabic nasal (p.1 minimal triple; Table 1 sorts all 592 tones of a text into H/M/low; H, M written, unmarked = low). Reports Momo 1950 '3 tons', Tadadjeu & Tegomo-Nguetse 1972 '5 tones' (+HL, LH modulated, now on double vowels). No stress.

tone_statements.citation: Bird, Steven. 1999. Strategies for representing tone in African writing systems. Written Language & Literacy 2(1): 1-44.
tone_statements.quote: High tone is marked using an acute accent and mid tone is marked with a macron. Low tone is unmarked. ... In Dschang, downstep regularly arises inside words, whether in isolation or in phrasal context. Orthographically, a downstepped high tone is represented with a macron and is called ‘mid tone’. ... Example (2) gives transcriptions to illustrate a four-way tone contrast. ... For Dschang, one can analyse noun roots as being lexically H, HL, LH or L, although the surface forms come out quite differently (see Hyman (1985:48) for full details.)
tone_statements.locator: preprint p. 3 (sec. 2), p. 4 (sec. 2), p. 9 (sec. 4), p. 14 (sec. 4.3); journal pagination differs
tone_statements.summary: Orthography survey using Dschang: high vs low level tones, written acute/grave plus ! for downstep; orthographic 'mid' is a downstepped high; downstep (even double) arises word-internally; noun roots lexically H, HL, LH, L (Hyman 1985). No toneme count given; 30+ tone-marked forms. No stress info.

tone_statements.citation: Bird, Steven. 1999. When marking tone reduces fluency: an orthography experiment in Cameroon. Language and Speech 42(1): 83-115.
tone_statements.quote: Dschang has multiple tone levels which may be analysed with some abstractness in terms of high, low, and floating tones. Phrase-final low tones may be level or falling; following standard practice, phrase-final level low tones are transcribed L°. Downstep is found in Dschang, so after any tone there is the potential of a six-way distinction between H, !H, L°, !L°, L and !L. A seventh possibility, !!H, equivalent in relative height to L, has also been documented (Hyman and Tadadjeu, 1976). ... few other tone languages have such a complex downstepping system.
tone_statements.locator: preprint p. 11, section 'An Experiment with Dschang' > 'Background' > 'Dschang tone orthography'
tone_statements.summary: Underlying high vs low plus floating tones; phrase-final rising = LH on one syllable; a delinked (floating) prefix low triggers downstep; surface contrast H, !H, L°, !L°, L, !L (+ !!H); orthography: acute = high, macron = downstepped high, zero = low. Lexical and grammatical tone. Nothing on stress.

tone_statements.citation: Pulleyblank, Douglas. 1986. Tone in Lexical Phonology (Studies in Natural Language and Linguistic Theory). Dordrecht: D. Reidel. Chapter 2, 'The relevance of downstep for a phonetic component', 27-66.
tone_statements.quote: Dschang does not exhibit downdrift. ... Dschang does, however, exhibit downstep. ... And not only does Dschang downstep H-tones, it also downsteps surface L-tones ... To summarize, Dschang nouns bear one of the following lexical tone melodies: L, LH, HL or H. One-to-one left-to-right association, in conjunction with the phonetic rule of Final Lowering and the phonological rule of Metathesis, go together to produce the correct surface forms for nouns in isolation.
tone_statements.locator: p. 77, ch. 2 sec. 5 for the first three sentences; p. 83, sec. 5.1 from 'To summarize'
tone_statements.summary: H/L noun melodies (L, LH, HL, H) linked one-to-one; downstep of both H and L from a floating L (p. 95), no downdrift; contours barred in the phonology (falling L only phonetic, 'on a single mora', p. 80). No tone count stated; data from Hyman & Tadadjeu 1976, argued from alternations. No stress.
